strings.A bordo de Orion el aviso ante un evento: On board Orion the warning for a radiation event is given by HERA (Hybrid Electronic Radiation Assessor), the spacecraft's radiation instrument, part of its caution and warning system. EMMA does not read HERA and does not replace that warning: this panel comes from the solar events it receives (DONKI or the simulated scenario) and from the recorded dose rate. Slides from 2019 by the JSC radiation analysis group describe the plan at that time: an alarm sounds when the HERA threshold is exceeded; with communication with Earth, the radiation console decides whether sheltering is needed, and without it the crew shelters when the alarm sounds.
strings.Ninguna de las páginas leídas da la cifr: None of the pages read gives the figure of the HERA thresholds. Also read, not cited: “Artemis I Radiation Measurements Validate Orion Safety for Astronauts” (NASA, 9 October 2024), which repeats that the HERA sensor warns of the need to shelter. The figure of the thresholds was searched for again on 2026-11-01, in the 2019 slides, in the RadWorks poster (NTRS 20150021957; no record in the registry) and in NTRS, and it was not found: the slides say there is a threshold, not which one. EMMA has no connection with HERA or with Orion telemetry.
strings.se muestra; EMMA no recibe ese aviso y n: shown only; EMMA does not receive that warning and it does not change the risk

strings.Nota descriptiva y fechada: el 15 de oct: Descriptive, dated note: on 15 October 2024 NASA and NOAA announced that the Sun had reached the maximum period of cycle 25, and they expected the maximum to last about another year before entering the declining phase; in the declining phase, the same note says, fairly significant storms are often seen, though less frequently. It is the most recent NASA or NOAA note on the phase of the cycle that was found: what it says about the present is a 2024 forecast, not a measurement of today. The solar cycle charts of NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center, read on 2026-10-26, do not state the phase: the last month with a smoothed sunspot number is March 2026, with 94.4, and the later months come without one: the page gives them as data not yet available or not calculable. EMMA does not infer from that figure which phase the cycle is in.
strings.Buscada el 2026-10-23 una nota de NASA o: A NASA or NOAA note from 2025 or 2026 saying whether cycle 25 is already declining was searched for on 2026-10-23, and it was not found. The “Solar Cycle Progression” page of NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center does not say so in its text: it gives the updated prediction (on the web since February 2025) and the data in charts. The charts were read on 2026-10-26 in the data files they plot, and they do not state the phase either: only the last smoothed figure is copied from them, with its month, without looking for the maximum or its date. The note of the same centre of 9 August 2024 speaks of a daily sunspot number, not of the phase. Searched again on 2026-11-01 on nasa.gov and noaa.gov, and again not found: the service change notice of the United States National Weather Service of 27 February 2025 announces the updated prediction, without stating the phase; the presentation of that prediction on NOAA's website, undated in what was read, does not state it either; and the NOAA news address that was tried does not exist. The copied figure is still the one from the reading of 2026-10-26, with its month: the data already carry a later one, and copying it as is would say nothing about the phase.
strings.descriptiva: la proyección al fin de mis: descriptive: the projection to the end of mission still assumes a constant rate and does not read this note or the NOAA figure, and it does not change any level

strings.Ninguna fuente de NASA leída dice cuándo: No NASA source that was read says when sheltering from a solar particle event ends: the 2016 Orion article gives up to 24 h inside in some cases, and the Artemis II one names a threshold for recommending shelter, not one for leaving it. NASA's 2016 evidence report speaks of sheltering for the majority of an event that can last several days, without saying what ends it. A 2025 preprint, not peer-reviewed and with data from the RAD detector of the Mars Science Laboratory on its way to Mars and on its surface, not from Orion, considers the event ended when the dose rate drops below the trigger threshold of 25% above background; with that criterion, the shelter times of the events it measures range from about 5 h 30 min to about 3 days and 7 h.
strings.Buscado el 2026-10-23 un criterio de fin: A criterion for the end of sheltering was searched for in NASA sources on 2026-10-23, and it was not found: the 2016 Orion article only says that the evaluation included how to get in and out; NASA Science's Artemis II page gives no duration or exit criterion; the Artemis II press kit (page and PDF) only schedules a shelter demonstration; the 2022 NASA article speaks of a vest that would allow leaving the shelter and continuing to work, not of when the event ends. Also read, not cited: the RadWorks shelter design (NTRS 20170002287), which sets how long the shelters have to be able to house the crew; it is a design requirement, not an exit criterion, and its figure is not copied here because that page has no record in the registry. The Artemis flight rules are not public in what was read. Searched again on 2026-11-01: the 2019 slides of the JSC group say when to shelter, not when to leave; the 2016 evidence report does not either; and “all clear” returns nothing in NTRS about the end of sheltering. There is still no NASA criterion.
strings.se muestra como fuente; EMMA no tiene cr: shown as a source; EMMA has no criterion of its own for the end of sheltering and gives no notice of it, and neither the stay it already shows nor the risk changes
